title: The Odd Women: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: A Society of One's Own: Reading Gissing's Opening World

utterances.text: Welcome to The Odd Women Unpacked — a close reading of George Gissing's remarkable 1893 novel about women, work, and the fight for a life on one's own terms.
Gissing wrote at a moment when the question of what a woman might do with her life — professionally, romantically, politically — was not merely theoretical.
It was urgent, contested, and for hundreds of thousands of women in late-Victorian Britain, it was the central fact of their existence.
To help us read this novel with the attention it deserves, I have three exceptional guests.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic novel audiobooks than any living person — he comes to Gissing as a performer who hears the prose from the inside.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been reading novels as moral fables — stories of character tested, will weakened, goodness discovered.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as an anatomy of class and power — he will make sure we see exactly who pays the price in this world Gissing has built.
Let us begin with the world itself — the London Gissing opens for us, and the social machinery that grinds through it.
The thing that strikes you first, reading Gissing, is that he loves his characters with a kind of helpless generosity — even the ones he makes suffer terribly.
There is a passage — Virginia Madden, one of the novel's most touching figures, walking into Trafalgar Square after a moment of private anxiety.
And Gissing writes that she felt — and I want to read this exactly —
"a delightful animation, rarest of boons, gave her new strength."
Rarest of boons — the ability to simply enjoy an afternoon.
For Virginia Madden, a quarter of an hour of pleasure in the sunshine is remarkable enough to be worth narrating.
That is a measure of how narrow these women's lives have become — and Gissing knows it, and he makes us feel it without ever editorialising.
Oliver is right to identify Gissing's generosity — though I would call it something slightly more precise: a sympathetic exactness.
Gissing does not pity his characters in the condescending manner of lesser novelists.
He renders their inner life with such fidelity that pity becomes something closer to recognition.
Virginia walking in Trafalgar Square — smiling, interested, as though she stood there for the first time — that is not a social statement.
That is a portrait of a soul briefly at liberty from its own anxieties.
Gissing's moral imagination, at its best, is devoted to precisely that — the interior life of people who have very little exterior freedom.
I don't want to quarrel with either reading — but I think we have to be precise about what produces that narrow life in the first place.
Gissing is not writing a story about unfortunate temperaments or bad luck.
He is writing about a structural condition — what happens to women of a certain class when the economic floor drops out from under them.
Virginia's quarter-hour of happiness in Trafalgar Square is so tender precisely because we understand its cost and its rarity.
The phrase Gissing uses is devastating in its quietness — this is
"such a quarter of an hour — so calm, contented, unconsciously hopeful — as she had not known since Alice's coming to London."
Unconsciously hopeful — she cannot even afford to hope consciously.
The system has made hope itself a luxury these women cannot quite claim.
And then Gissing gives us the counter-argument — not in a polemic, but in a character.
Mary Barfoot — who is extraordinary — delivers what I can only describe as a speech that belongs in a parliamentary chamber.
She is laying out exactly what women must do, and Gissing gives her the full stage — no irony, no undercut.
She says — and this is Mary speaking, in full voice —
"I am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person."
She owns it — every word of it — without the slightest apology.
Coming from a Victorian novelist writing in 1893, that is not a small act of imaginative courage.
I find Mary Barfoot compelling, but I want to be careful about how we read her.
Gissing gives her wonderful speeches — but the novel also tests those speeches against what actually happens to people.
She insists that women must become, in her words,
"militant, defiant" — that she "must push her claims to the extremity."
These are bracing words — and I do not doubt their sincerity.
But Gissing is too honest a novelist to let the programme stand unchallenged by human weakness.
And that tension — between the ideal and the actual — is where the novel's real drama lives.
Edmund raises the tension — and I think it's real — but I want to locate where that tension comes from structurally.
There is a moment where Mary Barfoot is discussing Everard Barfoot's father — a man who felt his wife had held him back.
And Mary herself — this militant feminist — repeats without quite endorsing the verdict the patriarchy hands down.
She says —
"Rhoda, when one thinks how often a woman is a clog upon a man's ambition, no wonder they regard us as they do."
A clog — that is the word the culture gives her, and even Mary cannot fully escape it.
That is Gissing's social critique at its sharpest — not in the rhetoric, but in the contradictions his most enlightened characters cannot think their way clear of.
And Everard himself is a magnificent complication.
He declares himself reformed — evolved, even — above the common herd of men.
He says — with tremendous confidence —
"If I marry now, it will be a woman of character and brains.
Marry in the legal sense I never shall. My companion must be as independent of forms as I am myself."
Independent of forms — it sounds wonderfully emancipated, doesn't it.
And Gissing — with perfect comic patience — then shows us exactly what Everard Barfoot's independence actually costs the woman who encounters it.
Which is precisely where Gissing's moral realism earns its keep.
Everard is not a villain — that would be too easy.
He is something more troubling: a man who has constructed a progressive self-image that flatters his appetites.
Gissing understood — long before it became fashionable to say so — that ideology and self-interest are very comfortable bedfellows.
That is a remarkable place to pause — a novel that holds Virginia's fragile moment of hope in one hand, and Everard's confident self-deception in the other.
And at the centre of both is the question of what independence actually means — and who truly gets to have it.
Coming up: we turn to the woman who most fully embodies that question — Rhoda Nunn, and the remarkable, unsparing cost of her chosen life.

segments.title: The Margins of Respectability: Rhoda Nunn and the Cost of Independence

utterances.text: We've just been exploring the world Gissing builds — its institutions, its atmosphere, its strange cast of survivors.
Now I want to move to the figure at the centre of that world's resistance: Rhoda Nunn — and what independence actually costs her.
Rhoda is one of the great talkers in Victorian fiction — and I mean that as the highest compliment.
When she speaks, you feel the argument has been honed over years of quiet fury.
She looks at the Madden sisters — these three women adrift — and what she feels is not pity but something closer to prosecutorial indignation.
She says — and I love the precision of this —
"the crime that middle-class parents commit when they allow their girls to go without rational training."
Crime. Not mistake, not oversight — crime.
Gissing gives her the language of the courtroom, and she uses it without apology.
And notice what sharpens that indictment — it's not abstract.
Rhoda immediately translates the moral failure into an economic one.
"They are capitalists; eight hundred pounds between them. Think what capable women might do with eight hundred pounds."
Capital exists. It is simply in the wrong hands — or rather, in hands that have been deliberately disabled from using it.
The Madden sisters don't lack money. They lack the education and self-belief to deploy it.
That is not a private misfortune — it is a structural outcome, reproduced generation after generation.
I don't dispute the force of Rhoda's analysis.
But I think one must be careful not to flatten Rhoda into a mouthpiece for a programme.
What makes her interesting as a character — and Gissing is too honest a novelist not to show us this — is the gap between her doctrine and her experience.
When Barfoot is present, something happens to her that her principles have no vocabulary for.
Gissing's own sentence is quite devastating in its quiet way.
"It was not love, nor the beginning of love; she judged it something less possible to avow."
Something less possible to avow than love. One sits with that for quite some time.
That line haunts me precisely because Gissing refuses to name it.
Love — Rhoda could theorise about love, could place it within her framework.
But this — this perturbation that distresses and shames her — sits outside the map entirely.
And her response — she forces herself to stay away when he calls — is so recognisable.
We've all performed indifference when we're feeling the opposite. Even Rhoda Nunn.
I'd push back slightly on framing this primarily as an emotional irony.
Because what Rhoda actually articulates — when she has the language for it — is a politics, not just a psychology.
She tells Barfoot directly that her aim is not personal fulfilment but the protection of living women — now, today.
The passage is extraordinary in its blend of the practical and the visionary.
"I have no hope of sudden results, Mr. Barfoot. I should like to save as many as possible of the women now living from a life of dishonour;"

"but the spirit of our work looks to the future. When all women, high and low alike, are trained to self-respect, then men will regard them in a different light, and marriage may be honourable to both."
That word — honourable — does so much work. Marriage as it exists is not honourable. That is her premise.
I find that passage genuinely moving, actually — which is not the reaction I might have anticipated.
"No hope of sudden results" — there is a humility in that which disarms the polemicist.
Rhoda is not promising a revolution next Tuesday. She is planting for a harvest she will not live to see.
That is a very old and honourable moral tradition — quite regardless of one's views on the woman question as such.
Where I become uneasy is in Gissing's treatment of those who cannot or will not share her vision.
Monica is not stupid. She is honest — perhaps more honest than Rhoda about what she actually needs.
Monica's confession to Milly Vesper is one of those moments where the novel suddenly lowers its voice.
She's speaking in the dark — literally, she asks not to be looked at — and what comes out is raw.
She says —
"I can't go their way. It seems to me that it would be dreadful, dreadful, to live one's life alone."
The repetition of dreadful — Gissing writes it twice, and you feel both of them.
And then she names what frightens her most: Alice and Virginia. Her own sisters as a living prophecy of what she might become.
And that is precisely Gissing's structural cruelty — and I use the word carefully.
Monica's terror of ending up like her sisters is completely rational given the evidence available to her.
The system has produced Virginia and Alice as its outcome, and Monica sees them clearly.
What the novel forces us to ask is whether the marriage she runs toward is genuinely an escape — or a different enclosure.
Widdowson's letter — Edmund drew our attention to it — is instructive here.
That cascade of endearments — "My darling! My dear, sweet, beautiful little girl" — is the language of possession dressed as devotion.
I would not be quite so clinical about Widdowson's feeling, though I take the point.
The letter is excessive — one cannot deny it — but there is genuine vulnerability in its excess.
"It's no use telling me that I must not use these words of affection; they come to my lips and to my pen irresistibly."
That is a man who knows himself somewhat, even as he fails to govern himself.
Gissing is probing something real about the weakness of will — what the moralists would have called incontinence — not simply ventriloquising a type.
What strikes me across all of these passages is how the novel keeps placing women's bodies and faces as the ledger of the system's costs.
The scene with Fanny Wheatley — Everard attending her wedding — is almost unbearable in its plainness.
Gissing writes —
"At three-and-twenty she had possessed a sweet, simple comeliness on which any man's eye would have rested with pleasure;
at forty she was wrinkled, hollow-cheeked, sallow, indelible weariness stamped upon her brow and lips."
And then the four words that make the whole thing devastating: "And all this for want of a little money."
Gissing doesn't need a theory. He just points.
Rhoda can articulate a vision of what freedom might look like — but Monica is already running from its mirror image.
Which brings us, inevitably, to the question of what Monica runs toward — and what she finds when she gets there.
Widdowson's love, as we've glimpsed it in that letter, is intense — but intensity and possession can look very alike from the inside of a marriage.

segments.title: Trapped by the Wedding Ring: Monica's Fall and Widdowson's Obsession

utterances.text: We've been exploring what Rhoda Nunn sacrifices in the name of principle — and now we turn to a woman whose story unfolds at the opposite end of the spectrum.
Monica Madden enters marriage as an escape from drudgery, and finds herself trapped in something far worse.
Let's begin with the husband — Edmund Widdowson — because Gissing makes very sure we understand what kind of man Monica has married.
Widdowson is one of those characters who announces himself in a single look — Gissing doesn't waste a line on him.
There's a moment when Everard Barfoot catches Widdowson watching Monica shake hands with a visitor, and the passage is almost frightening in its economy.
"If ever a man declared in his countenance the worst species of jealous temper, Mr. Widdowson did so."
"The worst species." Not merely jealous — the worst species of it.
Gissing is a novelist who knows that taxonomy is comedy and tragedy in equal measure.
And then: "his fixed smile became sardonic." The man is performing normality while consumed by suspicion — that's the horror of it.
One must be careful not to read Widdowson simply as a villain, though Oliver's reading of that passage is quite right.
Gissing gives him a kind of tragic consistency — he loves Monica with a possessiveness born of genuine, if deformed, feeling.
The real charge against him is not cruelty but a failure of imagination — he cannot conceive of a wife who is also a person.
Monica grasps this with terrible clarity when she realises she must keep a secret from him for the first time.
She had not understood until now how terrible would be the prospect of living here for a long time with no companionship but her husband's.
A husband as the definition of solitary confinement — that is not villainy in the gothic sense, it is something colder and more ordinary.
Edmund is right that Widdowson isn't a monster — he's a product, and that's precisely the point.
He's a man of small independent means — just enough income to keep Monica at home, just enough idleness to watch her every move.
The institution of marriage, as Gissing constructs it here, is a legal and economic enclosure — the wife is property that anxiety has animated.
And look at what Monica's one act of resistance actually is — she withholds information about where an acquaintance happens to be.
That is the entire scope of her freedom: a small social coincidence she dare not mention.
And yet even that minimal act of concealment — Gissing says explicitly — "could not but have an unfavourable effect on her manner of regarding Widdowson."
The marriage begins to crack not from passion or betrayal, but from the grinding necessity of self-protection.
And what's so devastating is the resolution Monica arrives at — Gissing gives her this flash of defiant clarity.
"Their way of life must somehow be modified; on that she was resolved."
"Must somehow be modified" — the vagueness of it is heartbreaking.
She has no programme, no Rhoda Nunn to advise her, no leverage whatsoever — just the bare will to endure differently.
And then Gissing puts her in Guernsey, where she promptly falls into an intimacy that will destroy her — it's almost Greek in its design.
And the destruction, when it comes, is mediated through something almost farcical — a private detective following Monica through Bayswater.
Edmund, you wanted to talk about Mary Barfoot's letter — that moment when the catastrophe lands in Rhoda's world.
Yes — it is a scene of quite remarkable moral compression.
Widdowson arrives at Mary Barfoot's door, looking — we're told — dreadfully ill, and delivers his news without preface.
"My wife has left me; she has gone to her sister, and refuses to return."
Those two clauses — the fact, and then the refusal — carry the whole weight of a marriage's collapse.
But what is most interesting to me is what follows: he has employed a detective — a private spy — within the institution of marriage itself.
That is not the act of a jealous husband — it is the act of a man who has outsourced his trust to commerce because he has none left of his own.
The detective is the detail I keep returning to — it's not incidental, it's structural.
Widdowson literally monetises his jealousy — he purchases surveillance of his own wife the way he'd purchase any other service.
And what does the detective discover? Monica knocked on Everard's door — twice — and found no one home.
She is destroyed for a visit that didn't even happen — for a door that didn't open.
Gissing is showing us that Monica's guilt or innocence is entirely beside the point — the system of marital possession doesn't require evidence, only suspicion.
There's a bitter comedy in the specificity of it — the detective's report, the closed door, the second visit.
Gissing has a gift for the absurd apparatus of Victorian respectability — and here the apparatus grinds a woman to nothing.
Monica's response — refusing to explain herself, denying guilt but offering nothing — is the one act of dignity left to her.
She has already understood what Widdowson cannot: that explanations would change nothing, because the charge is not really about conduct — it's about ownership.
Which brings us, perhaps, to the ideological thread that connects Monica's story back to Rhoda's — and to Mary Barfoot's extraordinary challenge to Rhoda.
Edmund, you've been sitting with that passage from Mary — the one where she accuses Rhoda of losing her womanhood to theory.
It is, I think, the moral centre of the novel — and perhaps its most uncomfortable moment.
Mary Barfoot — who is herself no traditionalist, who has dedicated her life to women's independence — turns on Rhoda with something close to grief.
"You have hardened your heart with theory. Guard yourself, Rhoda! To work for women one must keep one's womanhood."
And then the devastating conclusion: "you are wandering as far from the true way — oh, much further than Bella did."
Bella Royston — who surrendered to seduction and destroyed herself — is now held up as the lesser error.
Gissing, through Mary's voice, is suggesting that the coldness of systematic principle may be as lethal to humanity as the weakness of the flesh.
I hear that reading, and I don't entirely resist it — but I think it's worth noting what it costs Rhoda to be what she is.
Earlier in the novel, Rhoda states her position with a kind of ferocious honesty that I find difficult to dismiss simply as coldness.
"I am seriously convinced that before the female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a widespread revolt against sexual instinct."
That is not the speech of someone who has lost their humanity — it is the speech of someone who has looked at the evidence and drawn a radical conclusion.
Monica is the evidence. Widdowson is the evidence. The detective is the evidence.
Though there's a glorious irony that Rhoda herself is, by this point in the novel, secretly longing for Everard's arms — Gissing doesn't let her off the hook.
The narrator tells us she "loved with passion, allowing herself to indulge the luxurious emotion as never yet" — while simultaneously considering the vast issues of female emancipation.
She longed, the narrator says, "once more to feel his arms about her" — but even thus she could consider the vast issues of the step to which she was urged.
That's almost the whole of human experience in a single sentence — the body wanting one thing and the mind insisting on another.
And Gissing refuses to resolve it cheaply — Rhoda doesn't simply capitulate to desire, nor does she become a serene martyr to principle.
She perceives — and this phrase seems to me exactly right — "more strongly than hitherto that not only her own future was involved."
The self-regarding certainty cracks — she must think of Everard, of his reputation, of consequences beyond herself.
That is what growing up looks like in Gissing — not revelation, but the slow, painful discovery that other people exist.
Monica confined, Rhoda conflicted, Widdowson surveilling — it's a portrait of Victorian gender relations that is by turns tragic and, as Oliver suggested, almost comic in its mechanisms.
Which is perhaps the perfect place to ask: what does Gissing actually get right about the comedy and the tragedy of class and gender — and where does his own vision fall short?

segments.title: What Gissing Gets Right (and Wrong): Class, Gender, and the Comedy of Misunderstanding

utterances.text: We've been deep in the claustrophobia of the Widdowson marriage — that suffocating domestic world Monica can barely breathe inside.
But Gissing is also — and this is easy to forget — a genuinely funny writer, with a sharp eye for the comedy lurking inside his own earnest social arguments.
Oliver, you've spent more time than most people alive inside the rhythms of Victorian prose — where does Gissing's comic sense actually live in this novel?
It lives in the gap between what his characters believe about themselves and what we can plainly see.
And nowhere is that gap more delicious than with Everard Barfoot.
Everard is the great self-deceiver of the novel — a man who mistakes his appetites for philosophy.
He has this magnificent theory — that intelligent men are simply doomed to marry beneath themselves.
"But most of us know that our marriage is a pis aller. At first we are sad about it; then we grow cynical, and snap our fingers at moral obligation."
The magnificence of that — delivered, I promise you, with absolute sincerity on Everard's part.
He has philosophised his own weakness into a universal law, and he's rather proud of the result.
And yet one mustn't be too quick to dismiss Everard as merely a comic figure.
Gissing takes seriously the underlying moral problem — that desire and duty are genuinely difficult to reconcile.
Where I find Gissing most acute — most honest, even — is precisely in these moments of weakness dressed up as strength of mind.
Everard's cynicism is real cynicism — corrosive, self-serving — but Gissing doesn't simply lampoon it.
He lets it stand as a recognisable temptation — one that a great many educated men of that era would have found uncomfortably familiar.
Recognisable, yes — but I'd say the comedy and the class critique are inseparable here.
When Everard talks about intelligent men being condemned to inferior marriages, the word 'inferior' is doing a lot of ideological work.
It means women who haven't had the education, the leisure, the cultural capital that money buys.
His tragedy is a system, not a fate — but he experiences it entirely as personal suffering, which is exactly how ideology works.
And Gissing — who knew poverty firsthand — sees this with devastating clarity, even when his characters cannot.
And then there's the moment where Everard turns his sights on Rhoda Nunn — and the comedy suddenly has a genuine pulse behind it.
Gissing writes that Rhoda's appearance made his nerves thrill and his pulse beat — and then Everard says, with his absolute best theatrical instinct:
"Now there's a woman! Look at her, Mary. Do you wonder that I would walk the diameter of the globe to win her love?"
It's absurd — and Gissing knows it's absurd — but he also tells us Everard was "not all in jest."
That qualification is everything — the comedy and the desire are genuinely, uncomfortably tangled.
That qualification is indeed the mark of a serious novelist rather than a satirist.
A satirist would let Everard be simply ridiculous — a target.
Gissing gives him the dignity of genuine feeling, however self-contradictory that feeling may be.
Which brings us to Mrs. Luke Widdowson — there I think the comedy is rather less kind.
Oh, Mrs. Luke is a creature of pure theatrical joy.
Listen to this entrance — one of my favourite sentences in the whole novel.
"The widow — less than ever a widow in externals — came in with a burst of exuberant spirits, and began to scold the moping couple like an affectionate parent."
"Less than ever a widow in externals" — Gissing fits an entire biography into seven words.
We know exactly how she's dressed, how she moves, what she smells like — without a single adjective spent on her.
And she arrives into a marriage that is already suffocating — which gives that "burst of exuberant spirits" a rather pointed charge.
Mrs. Luke represents what the novel calls freedom — financial independence, social mobility, the ability to simply go out.
Monica has none of that — and her husband intends to keep it that way.
So the comedy of Mrs. Luke breezing in is also a portrait of what Monica is being denied — and Gissing wants us to feel both things at once.
And Monica's response — when the pressure of the marriage gets too near the bone — is devastatingly economical.
There's a moment where she could say several true and damaging things to Widdowson, and Gissing writes:
"Monica could have said many things, but she overcame the desire, and laughed the subject aside."
That laugh is the saddest laugh in the novel.
It's survival strategy, social performance, and self-erasure — all compressed into one reflex.
That is Gissing at his most precise — and his most compassionate.
What he understands — and what I think his detractors miss — is that the prison Monica inhabits is partly of conventional expectation, not merely legal or financial constraint.
She has internalised the rules sufficiently that she cannot quite bring herself to break them — even when breaking them is the honest thing to do.
That is a moral tragedy, not merely a social one — and Gissing has the integrity to show it as such.
I'd frame it differently — the internalisation Edmund describes is itself a social product, a form of conditioning.
But I think we agree on the basic point: Gissing resists easy villains and easy solutions.
And there's a wonderful image of that resistance in Mary Barfoot — who senses that "things mysterious were going on about her" and simply has to wait.
"She could only wait, repeating to herself that the grand denouement decidedly was not far off."
Even the shrewdest woman in the novel is kept in the dark — not by stupidity, but by design, by the systems of secrecy that protect men's manoeuvring.
And yet "the grand denouement decidedly was not far off" — Gissing lets Mary say it with perfect comic dignity.
She's not humiliated by her ignorance — she's alert, watchful, expectant.
Which is — if you think about it — a very good description of the reader's own position in this novel.
Alert, watchful, and increasingly aware that someone in the room is pulling strings — including, perhaps, the narrator himself.
Which brings us to the question of how Gissing's own voice operates in this novel — the irony embedded in the narration, and where it unsettles his own apparent convictions.

segments.title: The Narrator's Irony: How Gissing Unsettles His Own World

utterances.text: We've been talking about what Gissing sees — his acute eye for class and gender and the comedy of misunderstanding.
But there's a separate question, perhaps a more unsettling one: how does Gissing tell it?
What does the narrator's voice do to the world the novel describes — does it endorse it, ironise it, or quietly dismantle it from within?
The thing I keep returning to with Gissing's narrator is the quality of the patience.
He doesn't tip his hand with an exclamation mark or an authorial wink.
He simply describes — and the description is the indictment.
Take the portrait of Widdowson's marriage philosophy, which is just — extraordinary.
"Never had it occurred to Widdowson that a wife remains an individual, with rights and obligations independent of her wifely condition."
"Everything he said presupposed his own supremacy; he took for granted that it was his to direct, hers to be guided."
That word — presupposed.
Gissing doesn't say Widdowson is a tyrant — he says the tyranny was so complete it never even rose to the level of consciousness.
Oliver is right to highlight the narrator's restraint, though I'd put a slightly different construction on it.
What strikes me about that passage is the moral precision — not the political argument, but the psychological portrait.
Widdowson is not a villain. He is a weak man with sincere convictions — which is, if anything, more damning.
Gissing tells us his raptures were "genuine enough."
"His raptures, genuine enough, were sometimes interrupted in the oddest way if Monica chanced to utter a careless remark of which he could not strictly approve."
That phrase — "the oddest way" — is everything.
The narrator doesn't condemn. He simply registers the absurdity with mild, lethal bewilderment.
I take Edmund's point about the psychological portrait, but I think we need to name what structure Widdowson's psychology is serving.
His daily routine for Monica — morning household cares, afternoon walks with him, evenings with a book he approves — is a property regime.
And what makes Gissing's irony so sharp is that he shows us Widdowson's disgust at Monica's professional past alongside his total dependence on her performing domesticity.
The narrator records all of this without flinching — and without editorialising.
That is a radical act. The refusal to soften it is itself a political statement.
And when the narrator does break through — when there's a moment of direct moral exposure — it lands all the harder for the restraint that preceded it.
There's a passage I've been thinking about — Barfoot's argument over what should be done about Bella Royston.
Rhoda wants to send a cold letter and a cheque and consider the matter closed.
And Barfoot turns this supposed principle of self-respect right back on her, in a sentence that just demolishes the position:
"The letter of two lines and an enclosed cheque would as likely as not plunge her into depths from which she could never be rescued."
"It would assure her that there was no hope."
Four words. "There was no hope."
Gissing lets Barfoot carry the moral weight there — the narrator doesn't need to editorialize because the character has done it for him.
That is precisely the technique one finds in the very best moral novelists.
The author distributes his conscience among the characters — and trusts the reader to find it there.
What I find notable is that Barfoot's charge against Rhoda is essentially a charge of illogic, not of cruelty.
He says she is moved by "illogical impulses — and certainly anything but kind ones."
Gissing is doing something extremely subtle here — he's showing that ideology, even a progressive one, can become its own form of coldness.
Edmund's put his finger on something I think is absolutely central to how this novel works.
Gissing's irony cuts in every direction — not just at the Widdowsons of the world, but at the reformers too.
Rhoda is the most intellectually formidable character in the novel, and Gissing shows her capable of a rigidity that mimics the very structures she opposes.
And this becomes almost comically visible in the scene where Barfoot slips a marriage ring onto Rhoda's finger.
The passage is only two sentences, but the irony is structural:
"Before she could guess his purpose he had slipped a ring upon her finger, a marriage ring."
"Rhoda started away from him, and at once drew off the perilous symbol."
"The perilous symbol." Gissing gives us Rhoda's consciousness in those three words — and quietly shows us how thoroughly she's inhabited her own ideology.
"The perilous symbol" — it's also very funny. In a dark way.
A man produces a ring like a conjurer and a woman of iron conviction treats it as if it were a live coal.
And the narrator doesn't wink at us. He just says she drew it off.
That same quality of the narrator's restraint appears in the Rhoda scene I find most quietly devastating — her burning of letters through the night.
Gissing gives us the action with almost no comment:

"From a locked drawer she brought forth packets of letters, the storage of many years, and out of these selected carefully perhaps a tithe, which she bound together and deposited in a box; the remainder she burnt in the empty fireplace."
"The storage of many years." That phrase carries a whole life, and Gissing drops it without ceremony.
She burns most of them. She keeps a tithe. The narrator doesn't tell us what she feels — only what she does.
And then she paces the room in her soft slippers until dawn, unable to sleep. Gissing trusts us to know why.
That scene is one of the finest in the novel, precisely because it resists sentiment.
A lesser novelist would have given us her tears. Gissing gives us her soft slippers on the floor.
It is the detail — the specific, unsentimental, physical detail — that achieves the emotional force.
This, I would argue, is where Gissing's claim to a serious place in English fiction rests.
And there's something else in that scene that I think matters enormously.
Rhoda is putting her affairs in portable repositories. She's preparing to be mobile.
For a woman in 1893 to hold her life in boxes she can carry — that is a kind of freedom so minimal it aches.
The narrator doesn't call it freedom. But the structure of the scene does.
What all three of you are describing is a narrator who trusts irony more than explanation — and knows that restraint is its own form of argument.

Which raises an urgent question for where we go next: if Gissing's narrator unsettles the world of the novel, what does that unsettling do to the marriage plot itself — the engine that drives most Victorian fiction?

segments.title: The Marriage Plot and Its Discontents: Realism Against Romance

utterances.text: We've been tracking Gissing's irony — the way his narrating intelligence quietly destabilises every comfortable assumption.
That irony cuts especially deep when it turns on marriage — the institution the Victorian novel was practically built to celebrate.
Edmund, I want to start with you, and with Mary Barfoot — because her relationship with Everard gives us one of the most quietly devastating passages in the book.
Mary Barfoot is, in many ways, the novel's moral centre — and that makes her confession about Everard all the more arresting.
She is a woman of formidable conviction, and yet she is not immune to the shock of personal disappointment.
Gissing gives her this moment of naked honesty, and it rewards reading aloud.

"I never experienced such a revulsion of feeling as the day when I learnt shameful things about Everard... Since, I have thought of him as I have spoken of him to you — as an illustration of evils we have to combat."
What strikes me is the word 'illustration.' She has transmuted grief into doctrine.
The personal wound has been sublimated — quite deliberately, one feels — into a programme.
Gissing does not mock her for this. But he does not entirely endorse it either.
And notice what Gissing does just before that — he puts in his own small qualification.
Mary herself says — and this is in the text — 'A man of the world would tell you that I grossly magnified trifles.'
She volunteers the counterargument and then simply... sets it aside.
That is brilliant characterisation. She knows exactly what the world will say about her, and she declines to be governed by it.
As a performer, I find that unspeakably effective — the character's intelligence working against her own position.
But we should be precise about what those 'shameful things' actually represent in the novel's social logic.
Everard's transgressions — never fully named — are the transgressions of a man with money, leisure, and impunity.
He can afford his vices because the structure of his class protects him from consequence.
What Mary calls an 'illustration of evils we have to combat' is not merely a private failing — it is the system made flesh.
And Gissing, I think, understands that — even if he cannot quite bring himself to say it directly.
I would resist reducing Everard to a class symptom, tempting as that is.
What Gissing gives us later — in that extraordinary letter from Marseilles — is a man of genuine complexity.
He is sitting at a café on the Canebière, writing to Rhoda — the woman he professes to love — while being quite candidly captivated by another woman.
He writes — and I find this almost comically self-aware:
"One of them is so strikingly beautiful that I cannot take my eyes from her when they have been tempted to that quarter."
He includes it in the letter. He sends it to her. There is either tremendous honesty there, or tremendous arrogance.
Probably both — and that is rather more interesting than a mere class villain.
Both — simultaneously. That is precisely it.
And the setting is doing real work there. 'The Canebière is the principal street of Marseilles, street of gorgeous cafés and restaurants, just now blazing with electric light.'
Gissing gives Everard the most sensuous prose in the novel — warmth, light, beauty, luxury.
And Rhoda, by contrast, is shivering by the fireside — Everard says so himself.
The geography is the argument. Two different worlds — and he inhabits his with entirely too much relish.
And then there is Rhoda herself — because the novel does something quite remarkable with her.
In Chapter Ten, she makes her position absolutely explicit — and it is a position that must have jolted Gissing's readers considerably.
She says — without apology, without qualification:
"I would have girls taught that marriage is a thing to be avoided rather than hoped for. I would teach them that for the majority of women marriage means disgrace."
'Disgrace.' Not inconvenience. Not limitation. Disgrace.
She is inverting the entire moral vocabulary of her culture — turning respectability on its head.
And Gissing writes it with complete seriousness. He does not wink. He does not hedge.
And yet the novel then proceeds to test that position with something close to cruelty — because Rhoda herself begins to feel the pull of what she has condemned.
Edmund — the scene in Chapter Twenty-Six, where Rhoda is brought to the edge of capitulation and cannot cross it — that is where the marriage plot becomes something genuinely tragic, isn't it?
It is the finest passage in the novel, I think — and the most painful.
Gissing gives Rhoda an impossible dilemma — not a sentimental one, not a melodramatic one, but a genuinely philosophical impasse.
She cannot verify Everard's innocence. She cannot seek Monica's testimony without humiliating herself.
And Gissing articulates it with devastating precision:
"Listening to him, she had tried to put faith in his indignant words. But it was useless. The incredulity she could not help must either part them for ever, or be to her an occasion of new triumph."
'An occasion of new triumph.' Even here — even at the edge of heartbreak — her mind reaches for the ideological victory.
That is not a failure of feeling. It is what Gissing admires in her — and what he will not allow to save her.
What kills me — as a reader, as a performer — is the grammar of that sentence.
'The incredulity she could not help.' The passive construction — she cannot help it. It is not chosen. It is suffered.
Her scepticism is not a weapon she deploys — it is a wound that will not close.
Gissing writes tragedy in the syntax, not just in the plot. That is a remarkable thing to do.
And yet we should hold alongside that the other impossible position — Monica's.
Because Monica is not theorising about marriage. She is inside one, and it is destroying her.
And she says something to Widdowson — very quietly, which makes it more devastating:
"I really don't think I can live again as we were doing."
Eight words of declaration. No theory, no programme — just an exhausted, irreversible recognition.
Rhoda articulates the feminist critique in full sentences, with argument and conviction.
Monica arrives at the same conclusion through lived experience — and Gissing gives her fewer words, because lived suffering tends to be less eloquent.
That asymmetry is not accidental. It is the novel's argument about who gets to speak and who merely endures.
The novel refuses resolution — for Rhoda, for Monica, for the marriage plot itself.
Which brings us to the question that may be the hardest one: what, finally, does The Odd Women demand of its readers — and whether Gissing's refusal to comfort us is itself a kind of argument.

segments.title: Gissing's Unresolved World: What The Odd Women Demands of Its Readers

utterances.text: We've been tracing the way Gissing dismantles the marriage plot — and what he puts in its wreckage.
Which brings us, I think, to the hardest question of all: what does this novel actually demand of us as readers?
I keep coming back to Mary Barfoot's great address in chapter thirteen — because I think it's where Gissing puts his cards on the table, and then almost immediately shuffles the deck.
She opens, brilliantly, by reading aloud an anonymous abusive letter — from some out-of-work clerk furious at women entering the commercial world.
And Gissing gives us the flavour of it — she read it all through — and then Mary's magnificent aside:
"his uncivil attack had a meaning, and there were plenty of people ready to urge his argument in more respectable terms."
That's a performer's instinct — you disarm the opposition by giving it air time, then you name its real constituency.
Mary Barfoot is the best rhetorician in the novel — and Gissing knows it.
Oliver is right about the rhetoric — but I want to press on where that rhetoric lands, because the crescendo of the address is rather extraordinary.
Mary says she doesn't care about economic consequences, doesn't care whether women crowd out men — she wants only that women be made strong and independent.
And then she arrives at this — and I think one must read it slowly:
"Let the world perish in tumult rather than things go on in this way!"
Now — that is not a measured reformist position.
That is something closer to the apocalyptic — a willingness to sacrifice civilisation itself on the altar of the principle.
One admires the force of it while remaining, I confess, slightly alarmed by its logic.
Edmund's alarm is understandable — but it is worth asking what conditions produce that kind of utterance.
Mary isn't endorsing chaos for its own sake.
She is responding to what Gissing has shown us throughout — a social order that produces what she calls the contemptible wretchedness of women enslaved by custom.
When the system is that total, that entrenched, then the demand for its overthrow is not hysteria — it is the only rational response.
And what Gissing forces on us — what this novel demands — is that we sit with that logic and feel its weight.
I would not quarrel with that reading of Mary — but Gissing sets against her, deliberately I think, the Everard and Rhoda strand.
There is a passage where Everard looks at Rhoda — this woman who has absorbed every principle of independence — and Gissing writes with his characteristic cool precision:
"She was armed at all points. She feared nothing that he might say. No flush of apprehension; no nervous tremor; no weak self-consciousness. Yet he saw her as a woman, and desirable."
That final clause — "yet he saw her as a woman, and desirable" — is Gissing showing us that Everard's gaze remains unchanged even when the object of it has been transformed.
Rhoda's armour is real — and it is still not enough to dissolve the old masculine appetite for conquest.
And that's precisely the trap Gissing springs — on Rhoda, on the reader, perhaps even on himself.
He has created a woman of formidable self-possession — and then shown that self-possession operating inside a world that still reads her primarily as a body to be desired.
The irresolution of that is not a flaw in the novel — it is the novel's subject.
Gissing refuses to let us leave with a tidy verdict about progress or defeat.
But the passage that I think every reader carries out of this novel — the one that actually haunts — is the scene with Widdowson and Monica.
Because whatever we think about the ideological arguments, Gissing shows us what the system does at its extreme.
The prose is almost clinical, which makes it worse — listen:
"A short cry of terror escaped her; then she was stricken dumb, with eyes starting and mouth open.
It was well that he held her by the garment and not by the neck, for his hand closed with murderous convulsion, and the desire of crushing out her life was for an instant all his consciousness."
"All his consciousness" — that phrase does not let Widdowson off with passion or madness.
It tells us this is what ownership of another human being actually looks like when the mask slips.
I will not soften that passage — it is devastating, and deliberately so.
Widdowson is not a monster in the Gothic sense — he is an ordinary man in whom the logic of possession has curdled into something monstrous.
What Gissing demands of us here, I think, is moral seriousness — not ideological verdict, but the willingness to look steadily at what human weakness, encouraged by institution, can become.
That is what the greatest novelists ask.
And Gissing earns the right to ask it — because he has given us characters we inhabit, not diagrams we observe.
Monica, Rhoda, Mary, Widdowson — they breathe.
That's the thing about realism done at this pitch — the argument lives inside the people, not above them.
I think that's as fine a summary of what Gissing achieves as one could ask for — the argument lives inside the people.

We've ranged across this novel today — from the crowded parlours where Monica's fate is sealed, to the typewriting school where Rhoda and Mary reach toward something genuinely new, to the violence that waits at the heart of the old order.
And through all of it, Gissing refuses to comfort us — which is, I suspect, exactly what the novel requires.
My deepest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, to Sir Edmund Leigh, and to Daniel Rosen — three readers who have brought their full intelligence and feeling to this extraordinary book.
And thank you — to everyone who has listened and stayed with us through the odd women, and the world Gissing built to hold them.

c2:p118.text:
In the meantime a threatening cloud had passed from the sun; warm rays
fell upon the street and its clamorous life. Virginia felt tired in
body, but a delightful animation, rarest of boons, gave her new
strength. She walked into Trafalgar Square and viewed it like a person
who stands there for the first time, smiling, interested. A quarter of
an hour passed whilst she merely enjoyed the air, the sunshine, and the
scene about her. Such a quarter of an hour—so calm, contented,
unconsciously hopeful—as she had not known since Alice’s coming to
London.
c2:p118.summary: With the sun breaking through, Virginia feels renewed; she walks into Trafalgar Square with the pleasure of discovery, smiles, enjoys the air and sunshine for a quarter hour—a moment of calm contentment and hope, such as she had not known since Alice's arrival in London.
c2:p118.best_quote: a delightful animation, rarest of boons, gave her new strength

c13:p122.text:
“Now see why. Womanly and womanish are two very different words; but
the latter, as the world uses it, has become practically synonymous
with the former. A womanly occupation means, practically, an occupation
that a man disdains. And here is the root of the matter. I repeat that
I am not first of all anxious to keep you supplied with daily bread. I
am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person. I want to do away
with that common confusion of the words womanly and womanish, and I see
very clearly that this can only be effected by an armed movement, an
invasion by women of the spheres which men have always forbidden us to
enter. I am strenuously opposed to that view of us set forth in such
charming language by Mr. Ruskin—for it tells on the side of those men
who think and speak of us in a way the reverse of charming. Were we
living in an ideal world, I think women would not go to sit all day in
offices. But the fact is that we live in a world as far from ideal as
can be conceived. We live in a time of warfare, of revolt. If woman is
no longer to be womanish, but a human being of powers and
responsibilities, she must become militant, defiant. She must push her
claims to the extremity.
c13:p122.summary: Mary launches a sustained attack on Ruskin and conventional femininity, arguing that only militant assertion of women's right to work across all fields can advance civilization.
c13:p122.best_quote: I am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person... women must become militant, defiant. She must push her claims to the extremity

c8:p127.text:
“It amounted to that. From quite a child, Everard was at odds with his
father. A strange thing, for in so many respects they resembled each
other very closely. Physically, Everard is his father walking the earth
again. In character, too, I think they must be very much alike. They
couldn’t talk about the simplest thing without disagreeing. My uncle
had risen from the ranks but he disliked to be reminded of it. He
disliked the commerce by which he made his fortune. His desire was to
win social position; if baronetcies could be purchased in our time, he
would have given a huge sum to acquire one. But he never distinguished
himself, and one of the reasons was, no doubt, that he married too
soon. I have heard him speak bitterly, and very indiscreetly, of early
marriages; his wife was dead then, but every one knew what he meant.
Rhoda, when one thinks how often a woman is a clog upon a man’s
ambition, no wonder they regard us as they do.”
c8:p127.summary: Mary explains Everard's early conflict with his father, his father's rise from ranks and desire for social position, his regret over early marriage, and notes that women often impede male ambition.
c8:p127.best_quote: Rhoda, when one thinks how often a woman is a clog upon a man's ambition, no wonder they regard us as they do.

c14:p111.text:
“You could hardly believe it, I dare say? I am a far more reasonable
being now. I have changed in so many respects that I hardly know my old
self when I look back on it. Above all, in my thoughts about women. If
I had married during my twenties I should have chosen, as the average
man does, some simpleton—with unpleasant results. If I marry now, it
will be a woman of character and brains. Marry in the legal sense I
never shall. My companion must be as independent of forms as I am
myself.”
c14:p111.summary: Everard declares that if he were to marry, he would choose an intelligent woman; but he explicitly rejects legal marriage in favor of a free union with an independent woman.
c14:p111.best_quote: If I marry now, it will be a woman of character and brains. Marry in the legal sense I never shall. My companion must be as independent of forms as I am myself.

c11:p11.text:
“Now could one have a better instance than this Madden family of the
crime that middle-class parents commit when they allow their girls to
go without rational training? Of course I know that Monica was only a
little child when they were left orphans; but her sisters had already
grown up into uselessness, and their example has been harmful to her
all along. Her guardians dealt with her absurdly; they made her half a
lady and half a shop-girl. I don’t think she’ll ever be good for much.
And the elder ones will go on just keeping themselves alive; you can
see that. They’ll never start the school that there’s so much talk of.
That poor, helpless, foolish Virginia, alone there in her miserable
lodging! How can we hope that any one will take her as a companion? And
yet they are capitalists; eight hundred pounds between them. Think what
capable women might do with eight hundred pounds.”
c11:p11.summary: Rhoda passionately condemns how middle-class parents fail to educate their daughters, leaving them useless and trapped; specifically critiques the Madden sisters' helplessness and squandered capital.
c11:p11.best_quote: the crime that middle-class parents commit when they allow their girls to go without rational training

c14:p141.text:
Certainly she thought with much frequency of Barfoot, and looked
forward to his coming. Never had she wished so much to see him again as
after their encounter in Chelsea Gardens, and on that account she
forced herself to hold aloof when he came. It was not love, nor the
beginning of love; she judged it something less possible to avow. The
man’s presence affected her with a perturbation which she had no
difficulty in concealing at the time, though afterwards it distressed
and shamed her. She took refuge in the undeniable fact that the quality
of his mind made an impression upon her, that his talk was sympathetic.
Miss Barfoot submitted to this influence; she confessed that her
cousin’s talk had always had a charm for her.
c14:p141.summary: Rhoda admits she deliberately avoided Everard after their earlier encounter because his presence disturbed her emotionally.
c14:p141.best_quote: It was not love, nor the beginning of love; she judged it something less possible to avow.

c10:p28.text: Everard’s eyelids drooped, and he did not speak for a moment.
c10:p28.summary: Rhoda clarifies that her immediate goal is to protect living women from harmful marriages, while her ultimate vision is a future where universal female education and self-respect transforms the possibility of honorable marriage.
c10:p28.best_quote: I have no hope of sudden results, Mr. Barfoot. I should like to save as many as possible of the women now living from a life of dishonour; but the spirit of our work looks to the future. When all women, high and low alike, are trained to self-respect, then men will regard them in a different light, and marriage may be honourable to both.

c11:p74.text:
“He loves me so much that he has made me think I  must  marry him. And
I am glad of it. I’m not like you, Milly; I can’t be contented with
this life. Miss Barfoot and Miss Nunn are very sensible and good
people, and I admire them very much, but I  can’t  go their way. It
seems to me that it would be dreadful, dreadful, to live one’s life
alone. Don’t turn round and snap at me; I want to tell you the truth
whilst you can’t see me. Whenever I think of Alice and Virginia, I am
frightened; I had rather, oh, far rather, kill myself than live such a
life at their age. You can’t imagine how miserable they are, really.
And I have the same nature as theirs, you know. Compared with you and
Miss Haven I’m very weak and childish.”
c11:p74.summary: Monica reveals her deepest convictions: she cannot accept the unmarried life embraced by Barfoot and Nunn; the example of her unhappy sisters terrifies her; she prefers marriage over solitary spinsterhood despite acknowledging her weakness compared to Mildred and Miss Haven.
c11:p74.best_quote: I  can't  go their way. It seems to me that it would be dreadful, dreadful, to live one's life alone

c11:p35.text:
“MY DEAREST MONICA,”—the missive began—“Why have you not written
before this? I have been dreadfully uneasy ever since receiving your
last letter. Your headache soon went away, I hope? Why haven’t you made
another appointment? It is all I can do to keep from breaking my
promise and coming to ask about you. Write at once, I implore you, my
dearest. It’s no use telling me that I must not use these words of
affection; they come to my lips and to my pen irresistibly. You know so
well that I love you with all my heart and soul; I can’t address you
like I did when we first corresponded. My darling! My dear, sweet,
beautiful little girl—”
c11:p35.summary: Widdowson's letter expresses overwhelming love and longing for Monica, with escalating passionate language and reproaches for her silence, revealing his emotional desperation and intensity.
c11:p35.best_quote: My darling! My dear, sweet, beautiful little girl—

c12:p83.text:
It was with no little curiosity that, on the appointed morning, Barfoot
repaired to South Tottenham. He had seen a photograph of Miss Wheatley,
but it dated from seventeen years ago. Standing in her presence, he was
moved with compassion, and with another feeling more rarely excited in
him by a woman’s face, that of reverential tenderness. Impossible to
recognize in this countenance the features known to him from the
portrait. At three-and-twenty she had possessed a sweet, simple
comeliness on which any man’s eye would have rested with pleasure; at
forty she was wrinkled, hollow-cheeked, sallow, indelible weariness
stamped upon her brow and lips. She looked much older than Mary
Barfoot, though they were just of an age. And all this for want of a
little money. The life of a pure, gentle, tender-hearted woman worn
away in hopeless longing and in hard struggle for daily bread. As she
took his hand and thanked him with an exquisite modesty for the present
she had received, Everard felt a lump rise in his throat. He was
ashamed to notice that the years had dealt so unkindly with her; fixing
his look upon her eyes, he gladdened at the gladness which shone in
them, at the soft light which they could still shed forth.
c12:p83.summary: On the wedding morning, Everard observes Fanny for the first time; her face is ravaged by years of poverty and privation; she looks much older than Mary Barfoot despite being her age. Everard is moved to tears by her modesty and the tragedy of her sacrificed life, yet her eyes still shine with gladness and tenderness.
c12:p83.best_quote: At three-and-twenty she had possessed a sweet, simple comeliness on which any man's eye would have rested with pleasure; at forty she was wrinkled, hollow-cheeked, sallow, indelible weariness stamped upon her brow and lips.

chanced to notice that the husband’s eye was upon him, and with what a
look! If ever a man declared in his countenance the worst species of
jealous temper, Mr. Widdowson did so. His fixed smile became sardonic.

c15:p135.text:
Of this coincidence Monica thought better to say nothing on her return
home. She could not be sure that her husband might not, at the last
moment, decide to stay at Herne Hill rather than incur the risk of her
meeting an acquaintance in Guernsey. On this point he could not be
trusted to exercise common sense. For the first time Monica had a
secret she desired to keep from him, and the necessity was one which
could not but have an unfavourable effect on her manner of regarding
Widdowson. They were to start on Monday evening. Through the day her
mind was divided between joy in the thought of seeing a new part of the
world and a sense of weary dislike for her home. She had not understood
until now how terrible would be the prospect of living here for a long
time with no companionship but her husband’s. On the return that
prospect would lie before her. But no; their way of life must somehow
be modified; on that she was resolved.
